param.name: table
param.label: Your table
param.help: A sample sheet or metadata table in your own format: Excel, or text separated by commas, semicolons or tabs, with one row per sample (or per library) and one header row. Decimal commas and Latin-1 or Windows text are handled.

param.name: sheet
param.label: Excel sheet name
param.help: Leave empty to use the first sheet. Ignored for CSV and tab-separated files.

param.name: header_row
param.label: Row holding the column headers
param.help: Use this when the sheet has a title or notes above the headers. Comment lines starting with # (as in NCBI and ENA submission sheets) are skipped without it.

**Early version.** The FAIRe mapper is new and still being improved. Check its results before you use them, and send problems or suggestions to the Galaxy Australia help desk (help@genome.edu.au).
-----

-----
**What inputs the FAIRe mapper can work with**
Start with what you have. A sample table is all you need to begin, and each other file you add will improve the result.
If you are not sure which of your files is which, start with **FAIRe mapper: identify your files**. It tells you what each file looks like and which field of which tool it goes in.
*The steps to create FAIRe-formatted metadata with the help of AI, in order*
1. **FAIRe mapper: propose mapping** proposes a FAIRe term for each column in your sample table. 2. You **review** the matches, as described under *Reviewing the matches* below. If you like, **FAIRe mapper: ask a language model** can answer the columns marked for review, and you then check its answers. 3. **FAIRe mapper: find primers** finds the primer pairs that your methods name, cite or give as sequences, such as "the MiFish primers", "Pochon et al., 2013" or "TAReuk454FWD1 (CCAGCASCYGCGGTAATTCC)". It lists each candidate pair with its sequences, target gene and reference, so you can check them and copy the right ones into your values for the whole project. 4. **FAIRe mapper: apply mapping** writes the FAIRe workbook, based on your review. 5. **FAIRe-fier** checks the workbook. You can then use the submission tools to submit it to your chosen repository - now in a FAIR format!
Each step apart from your review uses a separate Galaxy tool, listed in the tool panel under the name shown in bold. Search the panel for *FAIRe* to find them. In the rest of this guide, the tool names are in italics and leave off *FAIRe mapper:* at the front.
*The files you can provide, and the tools that work on them*
- **Sample table** (needed by the *propose mapping* and *apply mapping* tools). This is the spreadsheet you keep for your samples, with one row per sample or filter, including the controls, and one row of column headers. It can be an Excel file, or text with the values separated by commas, semicolons or tabs. Your own column names and formats are fine. If a title sits above the headers, set the header row on the form; comment lines starting with # are skipped. The tools will do a better job if you:
- put one value in each cell; - give units in the header ("Volume (mL)") or with each value ("1 L"); - keep a column that says which rows are controls, and what kind of control each one is (the tools cannot tell controls from samples by their names); - give the time of collection as a time (10:00), in its own column or with the date; the tool joins a time column to the dates, and asks for the UTC offset on its form; - use the same sample names as in your OTU table.
- **Data dictionary** (recommended, for the *propose mapping* tool). A data dictionary is a list of the columns in your sample table with a short description of each: what it holds, its units, and what any codes mean. Many labs already have one, as a ReadMe sheet or a table in their methods. It is worth including: the tool reads each description as extra words for its column, so a short or cryptic header such as "vol" or "T1" can still be matched to the right FAIRe term. On our test tables it improved the matching, most of all for tables with short headers, and the descriptions also go to the language model if you use one. Give it as a table, for example::
Variable,Description,Units Days frozen,Days the water was frozen before filtering,days Who filtered,Name of the person who filtered the sample,
or as one line per column, the format used in many Dryad README files, for example::
Days frozen: days the water was frozen before filtering
In each description, say what kind of thing the column holds (a person, a place, a date, a volume, a count or a code) and what any codes mean ("NC = negative control"). You can give a whole README, as the tool ignores lines that do not name a column in your table.
- **Methods text** (for the *find primers* tool). This is the methods section of your paper or protocol, as plain text. The tool finds the primer pairs it names, cites or gives as sequences, and lists them with their sequences for you to check. You can also type primer names or citations into the tool, one per line.
- **Values for the whole project** (for the *apply mapping* tool). These are things that are true of the whole study, such as the primers, the extraction kit or the sequencing platform. Give them as a table of FAIRe term names and values, in an Excel, CSV or tab-separated file::
term,value pcr_primer_forward,GTCGGTAAAACTCGTGCCAGC nucl_acid_ext_kit,DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (QIAGEN)
If you have more than one assay, add an ``assay`` column for the values that differ between them, such as the primers. Rows without an assay apply to the whole project.
To see which terms you still need to find, look at the *mandatory terms not covered* output of the *propose mapping* tool. Its *things to decide* output lists what only you can settle before applying the mapping: a sample name used on more than one row, controls named but not marked in a column, columns of notes, and times with no time zone.
- **OTU or ASV table** (for the *apply mapping* tool), one for each assay. This table holds the reads of each sequence or taxon in each sample. The samples can be columns (as in an ASV table, or DADA2's table with the sequences as row names) or rows (as in a published matrix of reads per taxon), or the table can be in long form, with one row per sample and sequence. A table that holds several assays, such as Wilderlab's, can be given once, together with the column that names each row's assay. The sample names must match those in your sample table, or be their Illumina file names (M108_S7_L001 for M108), or carry a prefix that every sample column has (S_M108 for M108).
If you curated the taxonomy, add a column to your ASV table that gives each ASV its curated name, and choose that column on the form (*Column of curated names*). The tool then writes FAIRe's raw tables, with every ASV, and its final tables: taxaFinal with one row per ASV, and otuFinal with each taxon's reads summed under its most abundant ASV.
- **ASV sequences** (for the *apply mapping* tool), if your OTU table names its sequences (ASV_1, ASV_2 ...) but does not hold them, as LCA outputs such as eDNAFlow's do: the FASTA file from your pipeline, whose headers are those names. FAIRe needs each sequence (dna_sequence).
- **Library table** (optional, for the *apply mapping* tool). This table says which sequence files belong to which sample. It can be your study's run report from ENA or the SRA, the SRA submission sheet, or your own run sheet. A list of your fastq files also works: one name per line, with or without a header, and an md5 column if you have the checksums. The checksum file a sequencing provider sends (md5sum's output, with the checksum and the file name on each line) is read as it is, and so is the CSV from Windows PowerShell (``Get-FileHash -Algorithm MD5 *.fastq.gz | Export-Csv md5.csv``, run in the folder of reads). The tool pairs the forward and reverse files by their read number (1A_16S_Fish_R1.fastq.gz and 1A_16S_Fish_R2.fastq.gz are library 1A_16S_Fish), and matches each library to a sample by its sample name, or by a library name that starts with the sample name (M159_16SFish matches M159). Where the files name a sample differently from your table (FB1 for *Field blank 1*), add a sample name column to the list and fill it for those rows. The tool then fills in the library IDs, file names, checksums and links to the archive records in experimentRunMetadata. FAIRe treats a library as one amplicon of a sample, so each lib_id is made of the library name, the assay and the run (M159_16SFish_LerayCOI_Fish16S_RUN1), and a library that holds the amplicons of two assays gets two lib_ids.
- **Taxonomy table** (for the *apply mapping* tool), if your OTU table keeps its taxonomy in a separate file. The tool reads rank columns (Kingdom ... Species), FAIRe columns, or a single lineage column (``k__Animalia; p__Chordata; ...``, or PR2 and SILVA lineages such as ``Eukaryota(100);Obazoa(100);...``). The ASV ID or sequence should be in the first column.
FAIRe's taxonomy terms (kingdom to species) are Linnaean ranks, so the tool fills them fully only if you've provided Linnaean classifications, such as NCBI or BOLD taxonomy, whose names typically carry Linnaean ranks. For other classifications, such as PR2, it keeps the genus and species, notes on each row that PR2 was used, keeps the full lineage, and leaves the higher rank terms empty. Add the PR2 version you used (for example PR2 v5.0.0) as otu_db in your values for the whole project.
- **Your own primers** (for the *build primer table* tool), if they are not already in the primer table that comes with the tools.
*Reviewing the matches*
The crosswalk is the table of matches that the *propose mapping* tool writes. It has one row for each column of your table, with the FAIRe term it matches, and it is where you check the matches and make corrections. Each match is rated for how certain it is: ``skos:exactMatch`` marks accepted and confirmed matches, and ``skos:closeMatch`` marks those to review.
Open the crosswalk in a spreadsheet or text editor. To confirm a match, change its row to ``skos:exactMatch`` by typing it over ``skos:closeMatch`` in the ``predicate_id`` column. To correct a match, change the term in ``object_label``. To stop a column being matched, delete its row. Then save the crosswalk as Excel, CSV or tab-separated text, and upload it as the input for the *apply mapping* tool.
Any column without a ``skos:exactMatch`` row is kept as a user-defined field at the end of sampleMetadata, unless you tick *Leave out columns that are not matched to a FAIRe term* in the *apply mapping* tool. The *mapping report* output shows the evidence and the other candidates for each column.
*What you may still need to add*
The mapper matches columns in your sample table to any FAIRe term, including the ones listed below. For example, it matches *Collected by* to ``recordedBy`` and *Run* to ``seq_run_id``. It does not search the methods text for these terms, as it reads the methods only for primers. For habitats, it matches a column such as *Habitat* but keeps the values as you wrote them. FAIRe needs ENVO labels and IDs, such as ``sea water [ENVO:00002149]``, so you will need to add these yourself.
The terms most often missing from sample tables are who collected the data and who to contact, the project ID, ENVO terms for habitats, library and run IDs (unless you give a library table), and anything else that is not in your files. The *mandatory terms not covered* output of *propose mapping* and the log of *apply mapping* list what is still missing.

-----
**About the FAIRe mapper**
The FAIRe mapper is the first part of an AI-assisted pipeline for turning eDNA data kept in a lab's own format into `FAIRe <https://fair-edna.github.io/>`_ format. To match your columns to FAIRe terms, it uses the FAIRe checklist (version 1.0.2, which comes with the tools): the term names and their common alternative names, each term's type, format and allowed values, and whether the term applies to each sample or to the whole project. The matching itself uses no language model. If you choose, **FAIRe mapper: ask a language model** can answer the columns marked for review, in place of a person. **FAIRe mapper: apply mapping** then writes a FAIRe workbook from the crosswalk you have reviewed (the table that pairs each column of your table with a FAIRe term).
The FAIRe mapper was developed by Oliver Berry (CSIRO), with Claude (Anthropic).
